summary: Discovery/demo focused on policy-driven rate limits, org vs project key scoping, bursting, and quota enforcement for a multi-tenant inference platform. Redwood AE+SE walked through Console, API behaviors, Optimize recommendations, and failover policies. transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2025-10-14 | Start: 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Owen Mercer (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Lumina CTO), Alex Rosario (Lumina Platform Eng), Samira Nadeem (Lumina Security)

Auto Summary (may be imperfect): Walkthrough of policy-driven rate limiting and quota controls. Showed Console live: org/project keys, per-route quotas, burst windows, fallback to smaller variant models. Discussed security and VPC requirements and next steps for pilot.

[00:00] Jordan (AE): Hi everyone, thanks for making time. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Maya (CTO): Maya here.
[00:10] Alex (Platform Eng): Alex on the call.
[00:12] Samira (Security): Samira present.
[00:15] Jordan: Great. Quick agenda — we'll run through console, show how org and project keys behave, demo rate policies, then Priya will show Optimize suggestions and some passive caching ideas, and we'll wrap with questions and next steps. Sound ok?
[00:30] Maya: Yep, go ahead. We're particularly sensitive about noisy tenants and want predictable cost.
[00:36] Jordan: Understood. Two quick qualifiers — do you want this to be hosted (Redwood API) initially or are you already leaning to Dedicated + VPC?
[00:45] Alex: We're leaning dedicated with a private control plane — need to show to procurement. But for the pilot we might accept hosted while we do an eval.
[00:52] Jordan: Perfect — we'll note that. Also curious about burst patterns — are there periodic spikes or one-offs?
[00:58] Alex: Mostly daily bursts around 14:00 PST for batch jobs, plus a weird onboarding day where new customers ramp up.
[01:06] Priya (SE): Thanks. Ok switching to screen, I'll share the Console. Apologies if the screen share is a little laggy.
[01:15] [01:15] Priya (SE): (Console) — This is the org-level dashboard. You can see total tokens, broken down by project keys. On the left is the policy editor. We use policy inheritance: org -> project -> route.
[01:32] Priya: Example: Org policy caps at 1M tokens/day, project A can have 600k, project B 300k, and a shared reserve for bursts.
[01:45] Jordan: One thing to flag — our model is token-first so quotas are token-based not request-count, that's important for cost alignment.
[01:55] Maya: Token-based works for us, but how do you handle variable prompt lengths? If one tenant sends long prompts, do they blow others out?
[02:04] Priya: Good question. We support per-project soft limits and hard limits; soft limits trigger throttling warnings and can be configured to drop or queue. We also do token smoothing so bursts are spread across a sliding window. So a tenant sending long prompts will hit its own project quota first.
[02:22] Alex: And org-level enforcement? If multiple projects add up over org limit?
[02:27] Priya: Org-level is enforced as the absolute hard cap. We also have policy priorities, so you can choose which projects get protected in overcommit scenarios. For example you can mark "payment-processing" projects as high priority so they get protected during org-level pressure.
[02:45] Samira: How do keys map — are keys scoped to projects only, or can we issue user keys? We need tight audit logs.
[02:53] Owen: Keys are hierarchical. Org keys can be used for admin ops; project keys are scoped to a tenant's traffic. We also support ephemeral keys and token-level metadata for tracing. Audit logs show key, route, token usage and IP (subject to privacy). Note: the transcript may say IPs sometimes as I P's.
[03:16] [03:16] Priya: Now I'll demo a rate-policy rule. (types) This is a policy: rate-limit 100 rps per project, burst 300 for 30 seconds, then back to smoothing. You can target per-route as well — e.g., embedding endpoints versus generation endpoints.
[03:34] Priya: Also you can configure automatic fallback policies: if a project hits hard limit on the preferred model, we can fallback to a cheaper quantized variant, or to a smaller family, which keeps service up but at lower quality.
[03:46] Maya: Can fallback be based on SLA tier? We want prod traffic to never be downgraded.
[03:51] Priya: Yes — you can tag projects with SLAs. Policies have selectors; so prod projects tagged high-sla will have higher priority and can be excluded from downgrades. Non-prod can be downgraded or rate-limited more aggressively.
[04:06] Alex: If we do Dedicated + VPC, does the enforcement happen in the private control plane or back in Redwood?
[04:12] Jordan: Enforcement runs in the runtime closest to the traffic — for Dedicated deployments the policy engine runs in your private control plane; for hosted it's in Redwood's control plane. Either way, logs and metrics are pushed to the Console you see here or to your preferred telemetry (Prometheus, Datadog).
[04:30] Samira: What about encryption and KMS? We need customer-managed keys for model artifacts and logs.
[04:36] Owen: We integrate with KMS/HSMs. In Private mode you can bring your own KMS for envelopes and for audit log encryption. We'll share the SOC2 and KMS integration docs.
[04:47] [04:47] Priya: Switching to Optimize — this is the recommendations panel. Based on your traffic pattern you can see suggested batching, KV cache settings, and quantization profiles. It will suggest turning on prefix caching for repetitive prompts which reduces token counts.
[05:03] Priya: Example recommendation: For your onboarding flows we recommend 0.5s micro-batching window and using a 4-bit quantized variant for non-prod to save ~35% on token cost.
[05:15] Maya: That sounds useful. Does Optimize auto-apply or just propose?
[05:18] Priya: It proposes; you can auto-apply to non-prod projects but auto-apply to prod is opt-in. We have guardrails. The recommendation engine is conservative by default.
[05:30] [05:30] Alex: We want burst protection for onboarding — immediate spikes when onboarding hits. How do you model that?
[05:36] Priya: Two levers — short burst windows with a larger transient allowance, and a dynamic reserve pool at the org level. You can reserve X tokens per day for spikes across projects, or reserve per-region resources. The reserve is consumed only when projects exceed their quota.
[05:52] Jordan: Also important — throttling behavior is configurable: 429 with Retry-After, queueing with latency SLO adjustments, or immediate drop. You can choose per-route.
[06:05] Samira: Any chance of silent failures? Our security/compliance team hates silent drops.
[06:11] Priya: We're generally explicit — we emit structured errors and trace IDs. The Console also shows real-time traces so you can see which key caused a drop. That ties back to audit logs.
[06:23] [06:23] Maya: How do we test these policies in staging before cutting over?
[06:27] Owen: We support canary rules. You can route X% of traffic to a new policy and observe. The Console has a canary toggle and a traffic-split visual. We'll demo that quickly.
[06:40] [06:40] Priya: (demos canary) Here I create a policy and set 10% canary for project B. You can watch token usage and error rates in real time. Also we snapshot logs for the canary period.
[06:55] Alex: Nice. For our procurement team we need commitments around latency and uptime under guaranteed capacity. How do SLOs differ for host vs dedicated?
[07:05] Jordan: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed throughput targets, and predictable latency because the GPU pool is reserved. Hosted has best-effort latency with regional routing. For procurement we provide the SLA language in the contract — we'll attach example SLAs in the follow-up.
[07:18] Samira: On the audit side we need immutable logs for 12 months. Is that supported?
[07:23] Owen: Yes, and for Private we can ship logs to your storage. For hosted we can provide long-term retention as an add-on. Logs are tamper-evident and include key, route, model, token counts, and actions.
[07:38] [07:38] Priya: Quick demo of rate-limiter in action. I'll run a synthetic spike against project key. You might see some garbled words in the transcription later — real-time captions are lossy.
[07:46] [07:46] (sound of keyboard, test traffic)
[07:58] Priya: Ok you can see project hit soft limit then hard limit; the Console shows per-key graphs, and the policy editor highlights the rule that fired. 429 responses include Retry-After and a trace-id.
[08:12] Maya: Can we map those trace-ids back to our internal user IDs?
[08:16] Priya: Yes — you can attach metadata at request-time (header or token metadata) and we persist that in logs for tracing. There's PII handling options to redact if needed.
[08:27] Alex: Does Redwood support per-API-route quotas? We want embeddings to be counted separately from text gen.
[08:33] Priya: Absolutely. The route selector is path and model family aware — you can set independent quotas for embeddings, generation and reranking.
[08:41] [08:41] Jordan: Quick aside — regarding cost allocation, the Console has a billing export that breaks down token spend by project and by user metadata tag. This helps with chargeback.
[08:54] Samira: Any known gaps vs competitors? We heard from one vendor that they don't have per-tenant burst pools.
[08:59] Jordan: Historically some vendors focus on simple rate limits only. Our differentiator is hierarchical policies, dynamic reserves, and model fallback policies plus first-class private deployment support. But we do see Anthropic and Bedrock mentioned as alternatives.
[09:15] Maya: For the pilot we need a runbook: how to onboard, what metrics we measure, success criteria. Can you propose that?
[09:22] Jordan: Yes — typical pilot runbook: 4-week pilot, week 1 baseline data + small integration, week 2 perf run (benchmarks), week 3 policy tuning, week 4 evaluation + SOW. Success criteria usually are: latency <X ms p95 under expected load, cost per 1k tokens within Y% of projection, zero prod incidents for protected projects. We'll send a tailored SOW.
[09:46] Alex: On benchmarks — can Redwood run our real traffic patterns or do we need to synthetic?
[09:51] Priya: We can run both. For Dedicated we can test in your environment or in a mirrored environment. We'll ask for representative payloads.
[09:59] Samira: A procurement question — do you provide a PO-friendly invoice and net-60?
[10:04] Jordan: Yes enterprise billing options are available; we'll connect your procurement rep with our finance team.
[10:10] [10:10] Maya: Anything else on quotas? We have edge-case: partner tenants that should be rate-limited per-region.
[10:16] Priya: Regions are first-class. Policies can be region-scoped so you can place limits per-aws-region or per-data-center. For Private we map to your on-prem zones.
[10:27] Alex: Can we have overlapping policies? e.g., global org rule plus a per-project emergency throttle?
[10:33] Priya: Yes — policy evaluation order is deterministic: project overrides org unless you mark org as immutable. You can also set conditional rules via tags — so an emergency throttle can preempt normal behavior with higher priority.
[10:46] [10:46] (brief pause)
[10:50] Jordan: Ok wrapping — recap: we'll send SOC2 and KMS docs, draft pilot SOW, and schedule a perf benchmark. Maya/Alex to share traffic matrix. Any blockers?
[10:59] Maya: None from our side, just timing with procurement.
[11:03] Alex: We'll send traffic samples by Tuesday.
[11:06] Samira: I'll review security docs and flag any gaps.
[11:09] Jordan: Great. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the materials and calendar invites.
[11:16] (call ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings: "KV cache" rendered as "K V cache", "VPC" as "V P C" in some lines; speaker alignment is approximate.
